newsitem.title: INDIA: Asian leaders saddened by deadly haj fire.
newsitem.headline: Asian leaders saddened by deadly haj fire.

text.p: South Asian leaders expressed shock and great sadness on Wednesday over the fire in Saudi Arabia that killed more than 200 Moslem haj pilgrims, many of them from their own countries.

As many as 131 of the 217 victims of the blaze that swept through a sea of tents near the holy city of Mecca on Tuesday were believed to have come from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, diplomats and foreign ministry officials said.
Two Sri Lankans were also thought to be among the dead, the Foreign Ministry in Colombo said on Wednesday.
The dead were among some two million Moslems from 100 countries gathering for the annual haj pilgrimage, which reaches its climax on Wednesday.
Diplomats in Saudia Arabia charged with finding any bodies of their nationals and carrying out painful logistics expressed frustration over the lack of fresh information on casualties.

"All our efforts to get an idea of the number of dead are in vain. Hospital staff are not authorised to speak and Saudi authorities are not sharing new information with the embassies or press," one diplomat said.
In India, whose 926 million population is nearly 12 percent Moslem, Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda said he was deeply aggrieved by the tragedy.

"The prime minister has expressed deep grief and anguish over...the devastating fire in which a large number of pilgrims from India and other countries lost their lives," said a statement from the prime minister's office.
India's ambassador in Riyadh, Mohammad Hamad Ansari, said on Tuesday that more than 100 Indian pilgrims were believed to have died in the fire.
In New Delhi, a Foreign Ministry official in charge of an emergency haj unit set up to handle enquiries said two tents sheltering Indians were gutted in the fire.

"Their camp number 59, which had roughly 100 Indians in it, was completely charred, but we can't say how many people exactly died," he said. "Identification of the dead will commence on April 19, when the pilgrims come back from Mount Arafat."
Praying at Mount Arafat, where the Prophet Mohammad gave his last sermon 14 centuries ago, marks the climax of haj.
A Foreign Ministry official in Islamabad said 12 of at least 30 Pakistanis killed by the fire had been identified so far.
Scores of people gathered at the main Haj centre that handles pilgrims from Islamabad and Rawalpindi to inquire about the fate of relatives performing haj.
"I am extremely worried about my father who has gone for haj," said Saqib Adnan.
Pakistan's director Haj Aftab Zaidi said about 123,000 Pakistanis had gone on this year's haj.
Punjab province's chief minister Shahbaz Sharif expressed his "deep sense of shock and grief" at the loss of life.
Bangladesh's official news agency BSS said it had received a report from the embassy in Saudi Arabia that only one of its citizens had been killed in the fire.
The country's prime minister was one of those who left for Mecca on Monday to perform haj, accompanied by the religious affairs minister and other senior ministry officials.
"Bangladeshis (except for the one victim) are all safe and Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina herself is supervising their welfare," the embassy report said.

An official at Jakarta's haj coordinating post said Indonesian pilgrims were staying about five km (three miles) away. "It is not possible for them to have become victims," the official, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters.
Indonesia, most of whose more than 200 million people are Moslem, sent 200,000 pilgrims to the haj this year.
Pakistan's Zaidi said the bodies of its fire victims would be buried in Saudi Arabia.
"People prefer that their relatives are buried there in the holy land and the bodies are not in a condition to be brought back here," he said.
